contradictions.question: How should publicans be treated?
contradictions.summary: The Gospels can't agree on how Jesus' followers should treat tax collectors. The Synoptics paint Jesus as the friend of publicans, eating and drinking with them as a deliberate boundary-crossing gesture (Mark 2:15-16; Matt 9:10-11; Luke 15:1-2). Matthew 18:17 then turns around and tells believers to treat the unrepentant brother like "a heathen man and a publican" — i.e., as an outsider to shun. The same gospel that calls Jesus a friend of publicans uses "publican" as the shorthand for the person you cut off.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction is real and it sits inside Matthew specifically. In Matthew 9 and 11 the evangelist preserves the Q/Markan tradition of Jesus the friend of tax collectors — a tradition virtually all critical scholars (Sanders, Meier, Crossan) treat as historically secure because it satisfies the criterion of embarrassment. By Matthew 18, the same author is putting community-discipline rules into Jesus' mouth that use "publican" as a synonym for "outsider to be shunned." The apologist playbook on this one usually runs through Blomberg or Carson, who argue Matthew 18:17 is using "publican" as cultural shorthand — i.e., Jesus is meeting his Jewish audience where they are and the term is descriptive of how Jews viewed tax collectors, not prescriptive of how disciples should now treat them. That harmonization works rhetorically but it ignores the actual instruction in the verse: "let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican." The grammar makes the publican the model of how to treat the offender, not just an example of social perception. Critical scholarship (Luz, Davies-Allison) reads Matthew 18:15-17 as a Matthean redactional insertion reflecting late first-century church-discipline practice, retrojected onto Jesus. That is of course a redaction-critical judgment, but the tension between "friend of publicans" and "shun him like a publican" doesn't dissolve just because you label one verse cultural and the other ethical. Take your pick: either Jesus radically welcomed publicans, or the community shuns people "like" publicans. The text gives you both.

contradictions.question: Was Jairus's daughter alive when Jesus was approached?
contradictions.summary: Mark 5:22-23 and Luke 8:41-42 have the synagogue ruler (Mark and Luke name him Jairus) come to Jesus while his daughter is still alive — "at the point of death" / "a dying." Matthew 9:18 has the same ruler approach Jesus and announce that his daughter is "even now dead" (Greek *arti eteleutēsen*). The same scene, the same petitioner, two incompatible reports about whether the girl was alive or already dead at the moment of the request.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleanest demonstrations of Matthean redactional compression in the Synoptic problem. Mark's version (the source) runs the story in two stages: Jairus comes while the daughter is dying, then messengers arrive partway through to report she has died (Mark 5:35). Luke follows Mark almost exactly. Matthew collapses the two stages into one — by the time the ruler speaks, the daughter is already dead. The apologist harmonization (Archer, Geisler-Howe) argues that Matthew is just "summarizing" or "telescoping" the events, and that the ruler's statement reflects his certainty that by now she must be dead. That reading works only if you ignore the Greek. Matthew uses *arti eteleutēsen* — "she just died" — an aorist of immediate completion, not a hypothetical. The ruler is reporting a death, not predicting one. Critical scholarship (Davies-Allison, Luz, Hagner) reads this as a deliberate Matthean abbreviation that serves a narrative purpose: it makes the miracle bigger (raising from death rather than healing the dying) and removes the messenger-interruption that complicated Mark's narrative. The harmonization that the ruler "assumed" she had died by the time he reached Jesus is post-hoc rationalization — the text says he reported a death, not a probable death. That is of course a judgment about Greek tense, but the tense is what it is.

contradictions.question: When was the woman who touched Jesus's robe cured?
contradictions.summary: Mark 5:29 and Luke 8:44 say the bleeding stopped "immediately" — *euthys* in Mark, *parachrema* in Luke — at the instant she touched Jesus' garment. Matthew 9:22 says the woman "was made whole from that hour" (*apo tēs hōras ekeinēs*), explicitly placing the healing after Jesus turns and speaks to her, not at the moment of contact. Mark and Luke have a contact-cure; Matthew has a word-cure.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction sits in the Greek. Mark's narrative is unmistakable: she touches the garment, immediately the flow of blood dries up, Jesus *then* feels power leave him and asks who touched him. The healing precedes the conversation. Luke follows Mark verbatim. Matthew compresses the story and reverses the order — Jesus turns, sees her, says "Daughter, be of good comfort; thy faith hath made thee whole," and *then* she is healed "from that hour." The apologist response (Blomberg, Carson) typically argues that Matthew is just emphasizing that the healing was "confirmed" by Jesus' word, or that *apo tēs hōras ekeinēs* is an idiom that doesn't fix the precise moment. The first move is special pleading — Matthew clearly places the cure after the speech act because that's how he wants to emphasize Jesus' verbal authority. The second move runs into the parallel construction: Matthew uses the same *apo tēs hōras ekeinēs* formula at 15:28 and 17:18, both contexts where the healing demonstrably follows the speech-act of Jesus. The most parsimonious reading, and the one mainstream critical scholarship adopts (Davies-Allison, Luz, Hagner), is that Matthew is reshaping Mark to foreground Jesus' authoritative word rather than tactile contact — a theological edit that creates the inconsistency. The contradiction is small but it is real and it is in the source-text grammar.

contradictions.question: What were the names of the apostles?
contradictions.summary: The New Testament gives four lists of the Twelve (Matt 10:2-4; Mark 3:14-19; Luke 6:13-16; Acts 1:13) and they don't match. Matthew and Mark name "Thaddaeus" (or in some Matthean manuscripts "Lebbaeus whose surname was Thaddaeus"); Luke and Acts replace this figure with "Judas the brother of James"; and Simon is called "the Cananaean" in Matthew/Mark and "the Zealot" in Luke/Acts. The lists overlap on nine names but disagree on the tenth slot, which is filled by two different names.
contradictions.commentary: The harmonization is older than the apologetics industry — Eusebius already noticed it. The standard apologist move (Archer, Geisler-Howe, Carson) is to argue that Thaddaeus and Judas son of James are the same person under different names, the same way Simon Peter, Cephas, and Bar-Jonah are all the same guy. Plausible enough on its face — Semitic-speaking first-century Jews often had a Greek name and an Aramaic name. The Cananaean/Zealot variation is even easier: "Cananaean" is the Aramaic *qan'ana'* ("zealous one"), and Luke just translated it for his Greek audience. That part is genuinely defensible. But the Thaddaeus/Judas harmonization has a problem critical scholarship (Meier, Bauckham) consistently flags: there is no independent attestation that Thaddaeus was ever called Judas, and no first-century source explains the double name. Worse, Matthew's textual tradition itself can't make up its mind — Codex Bezae and the Old Latin read "Lebbaeus," while the Alexandrian witnesses read "Thaddaeus," and a conflated reading "Lebbaeus called Thaddaeus" appears in the Byzantine text. NA28 prints "Thaddaeus" but the apparatus shows the early church was already trying to harmonize the lists. Meier's conclusion in *A Marginal Jew* Vol. 3 is the parsimonious one: the precise membership of the Twelve was already fluid by the time the Synoptic tradition crystallized, and the gospel writers were preserving competing local traditions. The harmonization that all the names refer to one person works for the easy cases (Simon/Cephas, Cananaean/Zealot) but it's special pleading for Thaddaeus/Judas. That is of course a judgment call about how much harmonization the evidence supports, but the textual apparatus itself is the receipt.

contradictions.question: Should the gospel be preached to everyone?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 10:5-6 and 15:24 have Jesus restrict his and his disciples' mission to "the lost sheep of the house of Israel" — explicitly forbidding any approach to Gentiles or Samaritans. Matthew 28:19 and Mark 16:15 reverse this completely, commanding the disciples to teach "all nations" and preach to "every creature." Acts and Paul then turn the gospel-to-Gentiles into the organizing program of the early movement. The pre-Easter Jesus restricts the mission; the post-Easter Jesus universalizes it.
contradictions.commentary: This isn't really one contradiction — it's the editorial fault line that runs through Matthew's gospel, and critical scholarship (Davies-Allison, Luz, Meier) treats it as one of the clearest windows into Matthean redaction. The Matthew 10 and 15 sayings preserve an older Jewish-Christian tradition where Jesus' mission was understood as the eschatological restoration of Israel; the Matthew 28 Great Commission is widely held to be a Matthean composition reflecting the post-70 CE Gentile turn of the community. The apologist response (Blomberg, Carson, Köstenberger) is to argue "phased mission" — Jesus restricted the *pre-resurrection* mission to Israel because the salvation-historical sequence required Israel first, then the Gentiles, but always intended the Gentile mission. That works as theology but it doesn't dissolve the textual problem: Matthew 15:24 has Jesus telling a Gentile woman to her face that he is "not sent" except to Israel, and the saying carries no qualifier about phases. Mark 16:15 is also a textual time bomb — the Longer Ending of Mark (16:9-20) is absent from Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and the earliest Syriac and Armenian witnesses, and is universally treated by critical text-criticism (Metzger, Ehrman, Aland) as a second-century addition. Citing Mark 16:15 as Jesus' command is citing a verse Jesus' earliest gospel didn't contain. The most parsimonious reading is that the early Jesus movement was a Jewish renewal movement that became a Gentile mission after Paul, and the gospel writers retrojected the Gentile-mission mandate onto Jesus to authorize what was already happening. That's the consensus across mainstream scholarship — Meier, Sanders, Fredriksen all converge on it. Take your pick: either Jesus directly contradicted himself within a single gospel, or Matthew preserved an older restrictive tradition while adding a universalizing redaction at the end.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus tell his apostles to go barefoot and without a staff?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 10:10 and Luke 9:3 / 10:4 record Jesus telling the disciples to take no staff and no shoes (sandals). Mark 6:8-9 records the opposite — "save a staff only" and "be shod with sandals." The same scene, the same instruction, three Synoptic Gospels and two incompatible packing lists.
contradictions.commentary: This is the textbook Synoptic-problem contradiction and it's one of the cleanest demonstrations that the gospel writers were freely editing their sources rather than reporting verbatim. Mark, the earliest, permits sandals and a staff. Matthew and Luke both prohibit both. The directionality matters: when Matthew and Luke independently agree against Mark, source critics look for a reason. The likeliest is that Matthew and Luke were tightening the instruction to match the more rigorous itinerant-prophet ideal already circulating in their communities (compare the Q Mission Discourse). The apologist harmonization, exhaustively cataloged in Geisler-Howe and Archer, is that the Greek verbs differ: Mark uses *airō* ("take along") for the staff, while Matthew uses *ktaomai* ("acquire/procure") — so Jesus was telling them not to *acquire* a new staff while permitting one they already had. This works for the staff. It doesn't work for the sandals: Matthew 10:10 explicitly says *mēde hypodēmata* ("nor sandals") in the list of things not to procure, while Mark 6:9 says *alla hypodedemenous sandalia* ("but having sandals bound on") — a present-tense participle describing their *current* state of being shod. The two passages describe incompatible departure conditions, not the same scene with different verbs. Critical scholarship (Davies-Allison, Marcus, Fitzmyer) reads the variation as redactional intensification — Matthew and Luke ratchet up the radical poverty of the mission charge to match the prophetic-charismatic ideal of their communities. The harmonization rescues the staff at best; the sandals are still a direct contradiction. That is of course a textual judgment, but the Greek participle is doing the work.

contradictions.question: Is there an unforgivable sin?
contradictions.summary: The Synoptic Jesus identifies one sin that will never be forgiven "neither in this world, neither in the world to come" — blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Matt 12:31-32; Mark 3:29; Luke 12:10). The post-Easter writings reverse the limit: Acts 10:43 says "whosoever believeth" receives remission of sins, Acts 13:39 says "by him all that believe are justified from all things," Colossians 2:13 says "all trespasses" are forgiven, and 1 John 1:9 promises cleansing from "all unrighteousness." One stream of texts excludes a sin from forgiveness; the other promises forgiveness without exclusion.
contradictions.commentary: The tension here is between Jesus' eschatological judgment-saying and the early church's universalizing soteriology. The blasphemy-against-the-Spirit logion is reconstructed by most critical scholars (Marcus, Davies-Allison, Boring) as a genuine Q/Markan saying with a polemical context — Jesus is responding to accusations that he casts out demons by Beelzebul, and the "unforgivable" charge is leveled specifically at his opponents who attribute the work of God's Spirit to Satan. The apologist harmonization (Carson, Blomberg, Grudem) is that the apparent contradiction dissolves once you recognize that the blasphemy in question is a settled, lifelong refusal to recognize the Spirit's work — i.e., it's unforgivable because the blasphemer never repents, not because forgiveness is intrinsically unavailable. That harmonization has some textual traction in Mark 3:29's qualifier *enochos estin aiōniou hamartēmatos* ("is guilty of an eternal sin") — implying a state, not just an act. But it requires reading the verse against its grammar. Matthew 12:32 explicitly says blasphemy against the Spirit "shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, neither in the world to come" (*oute en toutō tō aiōni oute en tō mellonti*) — that's a categorical denial of forgiveness across both ages, not a description of an unrepented state. The most parsimonious reading is that the Synoptic Jesus held a more restrictive forgiveness theology (consistent with first-century Jewish apocalyptic categories where certain sins like apostasy were unforgivable — compare 1QS 7:22-25 from Qumran and *m. Sanh.* 10:1), while the later epistolary tradition developed a fully universal forgiveness-through-faith soteriology. Both traditions are in the canon. Take your pick.

contradictions.question: Did John the Baptist recognize Jesus as the Son of God?
contradictions.summary: John 1:29-34 has John the Baptist not only recognize Jesus on sight as "the Lamb of God" but explicitly testify, "I saw, and bare record that this is the Son of God." Matthew 11:2-3 and the parallel in Luke 7:18-20 have John, later in his ministry and from prison, send disciples to ask Jesus the basic question: "Art thou he that should come, or do we look for another?" If John already knew Jesus was the Son of God at the beginning, the prison-question is incoherent.
contradictions.commentary: This is a genuine contradiction and it sits on the Synoptic-Johannine seam. The Synoptic Baptist is a fully human eschatological prophet who recognizes Jesus' specialness but isn't sure about the messianic identification — his prison-question to Jesus reads as exactly what it appears to be: doubt. The Johannine Baptist is a theologically loaded figure who functions as a witness-character in the Fourth Gospel's prologue-fulfillment structure; he sees the Spirit descend, identifies Jesus immediately and absolutely, and never wavers. Critical scholarship (Brown, Meier, Webb) has long recognized this as a redactional reshaping of the Baptist by the Fourth Evangelist for christological purposes — the Baptist in John exists to point to Jesus, full stop, and any human ambiguity has been edited out. The apologist harmonization (Carson, Köstenberger, Blomberg) runs through a few moves. First, that John in prison was discouraged rather than ignorant — he knew who Jesus was but needed reassurance. Second, that the prison-question was for the benefit of John's disciples rather than John himself. Both readings require importing motivations the text doesn't give. The Matthean version explicitly attributes the question to John (*pempsas dia tōn mathētōn autou eipen autō*) and the question is direct: are you the one, or do we look for another? It is not phrased as a check-in or a discipleship-training exercise. The parsimonious reading, and the one Brown's AB commentary settles on, is that the Synoptic and Johannine traditions preserve incompatible portraits of the Baptist — one historically plausible (a prophet who recognized Jesus' importance but didn't necessarily fix him as the eschatological figure), one theologically constructed (a witness whose only narrative function is to identify the Son of God). That is of course a redaction-critical conclusion, but it's what the texts actually say when you stop trying to weld them together.

contradictions.question: Was John the Baptist Elijah?
contradictions.summary: In Matthew 11:14 Jesus says of John the Baptist: "this is Elijah, which was for to come," and Matthew 17:12-13 makes the identification explicit — the disciples "understood that he spake unto them of John the Baptist." Luke 7:24-27 confirms the same identification via Malachi 3:1. In John 1:21, the Baptist is asked directly by the Jerusalem delegation, "Art thou Elijah?" and he flatly answers, "I am not." Jesus says John is Elijah; John says he is not.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction is real and theological scholarship has been wrestling with it for centuries. The Synoptic identification of John with Elijah serves a specific eschatological function: Malachi 4:5-6 had prophesied that Elijah would return before "the great and dreadful day of the LORD," and identifying John as Elijah is how the Synoptic Jesus authenticates his own role as the Messiah who follows the eschatological forerunner. The Johannine Baptist denial serves the opposite function — in the Fourth Gospel, John's role is exclusively to point to Jesus, not to be a figure in his own right, and any identification of John with Elijah would compete with that single-witness theology. The apologist harmonization (Carson, Köstenberger, Blomberg, Morris) is the standard "two senses" move: John is Elijah in the *functional* sense (the prophet who fulfills the Elijah-role of forerunner) but not in the *literal* sense (he is not the bodily reincarnation of the prophet Elijah), and the Johannine question is asking the literal version while Jesus is answering the functional one. This is the cleanest available harmonization and it has genuine textual support — Luke 1:17 explicitly says John would come "in the spirit and power of Elias," which is functional rather than literal language. So at the level of intent, the harmonization is plausible. But it doesn't fully resolve the surface contradiction because Jesus, in Matthew 11:14, doesn't use functional language — he says *autos estin Ēlias ho mellōn erchesthai* ("this is Elijah, the one about to come"), which uses exactly the eschatological-return phrasing of Malachi. The Johannine delegation is using the same eschatological category. They're asking the same question Jesus is answering, and they get opposite answers. The mainstream critical reading (Brown, Meier, Davies-Allison) is that the Synoptic tradition preserves an early identification of John as Elijah-returned, and the Fourth Gospel actively suppresses this identification because by the time John was written, the church needed John's witness to be subordinate to Jesus, not parallel to him as a returning prophet. That's a redaction-critical conclusion, but it accounts for the texts more parsimoniously than the functional/literal split.

contradictions.question: Who is for or against Jesus?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 12:30 and Luke 11:23 record Jesus saying, "He that is not with me is against me." Mark 9:40 and Luke 9:50 record Jesus saying the opposite: "he that is not against us is on our part / for us." The two sayings frame neutrality as exclusion in one case and inclusion in the other. Luke records both, so the contradiction is internal to a single gospel.
contradictions.commentary: This is the rare gospel contradiction that the text itself preserves without trying to resolve. Luke includes both sayings, in different contexts, and doesn't reconcile them. The apologist harmonization (Carson, Blomberg, Bock) is the contextual move: the two sayings have different referents and different audiences, so they don't actually contradict. In the Mark 9:40 / Luke 9:50 context, the disciples have just told Jesus they tried to stop someone casting out demons in his name because he wasn't part of their group — and Jesus' response is the inclusive one: outsiders doing the work of the kingdom are allies, don't shut them down. In the Matthew 12:30 / Luke 11:23 context, Jesus has just been accused of casting out demons by Beelzebul — and the exclusive saying is leveled at opponents who attribute his work to Satan: there is no neutral ground when the kingdom is breaking in. This is a genuinely strong harmonization and most critical scholars (Marcus, Fitzmyer, Davies-Allison) acknowledge that the two sayings address different situations: tolerance toward sympathetic outsiders versus demand for decision against active opponents. The dialectic is even psychologically coherent — it's the same logic as "be tolerant of those who help you, intolerant of those who fight you." Where the contradiction reappears is when the sayings are quoted as universal principles, which is how both ancient and modern Christian rhetoric typically deploys them. Read as universal moral maxims, they directly contradict; read as situational responses, they form a single coherent stance. That is of course a contextual judgment. The text gives you both readings; the harmonization works at the historical-Jesus level but doesn't dissolve the surface contradiction at the proverbial level — which is how most readers encounter them.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus perform many signs and wonders?
contradictions.summary: John 3:2, John 12:37, John 20:30, and Acts 2:22 explicitly say Jesus performed many signs and miracles publicly. Mark 8:12 has Jesus refuse to give any sign at all: "there shall no sign be given unto this generation." Matthew 12:39 / 16:4 modifies the refusal slightly to allow one exception — "the sign of the prophet Jonas." Three positions sit in the same canon: many signs, no signs, and one sign.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction here is real but its shape depends on the technical use of *sēmeion* ("sign") in the gospel traditions, and that's where the apologist harmonization actually has some traction. The Markan and Matthean refusal-sayings are responses to specific demands from Pharisees and scribes for a *legitimating sign from heaven* — an apocalyptic public proof of messianic identity. Jesus refuses that specific kind of sign while continuing to perform healings and exorcisms throughout the narrative. So the apologist response (Carson, Blomberg, France) reads: Jesus performed many signs in the sense of miracles, but refused to perform a *sign-on-demand* of the apocalyptic-proof variety. That's a defensible reading and Marcus, France, and Hagner all acknowledge the technical distinction. Where the apologist harmonization runs into trouble is the Markan version specifically — Mark 8:12 has Jesus refuse "any" sign (*ei dothēsetai tē genea tautē sēmeion*), with no exception clause. Matthew 12:39 / 16:4 adds the Jonah exception, which most critical scholars (Marcus, Davies-Allison, Boring) read as Matthean editorial softening — Matthew is uncomfortable with the categorical refusal in his source and adds a typological qualifier. The bigger problem is John. The Fourth Gospel's whole structure is built around seven public *sēmeia* (signs) intended to produce belief, and John 12:37 explicitly laments that despite Jesus' "many" public signs the crowds didn't believe. The Synoptic refusal-sayings and the Johannine sign-theology are operating with different concepts of what "sign" means and different theologies of how Jesus authenticates himself. The historical-Jesus question — did Jesus actually refuse sign-demands, or did he perform public signs to authenticate his mission? — gets answered differently by different gospel writers. The parsimonious reading, and the one critical scholarship converges on, is that Mark preserves an older tradition of a Jesus who refused legitimating signs; Matthew softens it; John constructs a counter-tradition where signs are the primary mode of authentication. Take your pick which tradition you believe.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus have secret teachings?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 13:10-11, Mark 4:10-11, and Luke 8:9-10 all have Jesus tell the disciples that the parables function as a deliberate esoteric/exoteric distinction: "unto you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God: but unto them that are without, all these things are done in parables." The disciples get the secrets; outsiders get coded speech. John 18:20 contradicts this explicitly: "I spake openly to the world... and in secret have I said nothing."
contradictions.commentary: The Synoptic parable-theory is one of the most theologically scandalous passages in Mark — the Markan Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9-10 to say that parables exist specifically to *prevent* outsiders from understanding, lest they repent and be forgiven. Mark 4:12 makes this explicit: "that seeing they may see, and not perceive...lest at any time they should be converted, and their sins should be forgiven them." Matthew softens this by changing the *hina* ("in order that") of Mark to *hoti* ("because") — making the parables descriptive rather than causal — but the basic two-tier teaching structure remains in all three Synoptics. The Johannine Jesus, by contrast, repeatedly insists he has taught publicly and has nothing hidden. The apologist harmonization (Carson, Blomberg, Köstenberger) is that John 18:20 is responding to a specific accusation from the high priest that Jesus was leading a secret conspiratorial movement, and Jesus is denying *conspiratorial secrecy*, not denying that he taught some things differently to the inner circle. That reading has some textual support — the context is a legal interrogation about Jesus' "doctrine and disciples," and Jesus' answer is structured as a denial of a charge. But the language Jesus uses is sweeping: *en kryptō elalēsa ouden* ("in secret have I said nothing"). He's not saying "I didn't lead a secret political conspiracy"; he's saying he taught nothing in secret. That directly contradicts the Synoptic parable-theory where private esoteric teaching to the Twelve is one of the structural features of Jesus' ministry. Critical scholarship (Brown, Marcus, Räisänen) reads this as a Johannine theological move — the Fourth Gospel constructs a Jesus whose teaching is fully transparent because the Logos cannot be hidden, while the Synoptic tradition preserves the older messianic-secret/parable-theory motif Mark inherited. The two portraits are not really compatible without significant interpretive labor. That is of course a redaction-critical judgment, but Mark 4:11-12 and John 18:20 are saying opposite things in the same testamental canon.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus always speak in parables?
contradictions.summary: Mark 4:33-34 and the parallel in Matthew 13:34 make an absolute claim: "without a parable spake he not unto them" / "He never spoke to them without using parables." Taken at face value, this means every public utterance of Jesus was in parable form. The rest of the gospel record — the Sermon on the Mount, the Olivet Discourse, the dialogues with opponents, the Johannine "I am" sayings, the temple cleansing words — flatly contradicts this. Jesus speaks plainly in countless non-parabolic discourses across all four gospels, including in Matthew's own gospel.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction here is internal to the canon and even internal to Matthew. Matthew 13:34 makes the absolute claim that Jesus spoke nothing to the crowds except in parables; but the Sermon on the Mount (Matt 5-7), the missionary discourse (Matt 10), the woes against the Pharisees (Matt 23), and the eschatological discourse (Matt 24-25) are mostly non-parabolic public teaching to mixed crowds. So Matthew is contradicting Matthew. The apologist response (Carson, Blomberg, France, Hagner) restricts the absolute claim to a specific period of Jesus' ministry — the so-called "parabolic period" in Galilee surrounding Mark 4 / Matthew 13 — and reads the Markan summary as a literary closure of that specific teaching episode rather than a universal claim about Jesus' communication style. There's textual traction here: Mark 4:33-34 sits at the conclusion of a parable-discourse chapter and could plausibly function as a wrap-up describing *that day's* teaching mode. France, in his NIGTC Mark, makes this case explicitly. The harmonization is defensible if you restrict the saying to the immediate literary context. Where the harmonization weakens is the grammar: Mark says *chōris de parabolēs ouk elalei autois* — "and without a parable he was not speaking to them" — using the imperfect tense, which describes habitual or ongoing action, not a single day's activity. Matthew tightens this further with *ouden elalei autois* ("nothing he was speaking to them [except in parables]"). The most parsimonious reading, and the one critical scholarship (Marcus, Davies-Allison, Hooker) adopts, is that Mark 4:33-34 is an editorial generalization that overstates the case — a redactional summary that fits the parable-collection chapter but doesn't actually describe Jesus' full teaching practice. That's a redactional judgment, not a denial that Jesus told parables. The contradiction is between the absolute textual claim and the contents of the gospels themselves. contradictions.question: When was Jesus rejected by the people in his hometown of Nazareth?
contradictions.summary: Luke 4:13-30 places the Nazareth rejection at the very *beginning* of Jesus' Galilean ministry, immediately after the temptation, as the inaugural event setting the trajectory of his mission. Matthew 13:53-58 and Mark 6:1-5 place the same Nazareth rejection much later, after the Sermon on the Mount / parable discourse, well into the public ministry. The same incident — Jesus rejected in his hometown — appears at incompatible points in the narrative chronology.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the clearest cases where Luke and the other two Synoptics arrange the same source material in incompatible sequences. Mark places the Nazareth rejection in chapter 6, after Jesus has already amassed disciples, performed multiple miracles, and become a public figure. Luke moves the same incident forward to chapter 4 and makes it the programmatic opening of the ministry, complete with the Isaiah 61 "Spirit of the Lord is upon me" scroll-reading that doesn't appear in Mark or Matthew at all. The apologist harmonization (Carson, Blomberg, Bock, Marshall) splits the difference: these were two separate rejections at Nazareth, an early one (Luke 4) and a later one (Matt 13 / Mark 6), and Jesus visited his hometown twice and got rejected twice. That's textually possible but it requires multiplying events without warrant, which violates the principle of parsimony. The bigger problem with the two-rejections harmonization is that Luke 4 contains specific elements that critical scholarship (Fitzmyer, Bovon, Marshall himself partly admits) recognizes as Lukan editorial composition: the scroll-reading scene is unique to Luke, the citation of 1 Kings 17 / 2 Kings 5 about Elijah and Elisha is a Lukan theological motif (Gentile inclusion) introduced here as a programmatic preview, and the attempted-cliff-throwing is unique to Luke. Luke is shaping the Nazareth episode into a thematic introduction to his entire gospel — a rejection by Israel that prefigures the Gentile mission. The parsimonious critical reading (Fitzmyer, Bovon, Brown, Meier) is that Luke has relocated the Markan Nazareth pericope to the front of his gospel and substantially expanded it for theological purposes, in keeping with his broader redactional pattern of programmatic openings (compare the Magnificat, Benedictus, and Nunc Dimittis as opening compositions). The two-rejections harmonization works only if you're willing to ignore that Luke is doing the kind of literary front-loading that scholars can document throughout his gospel. Take your pick: either there were two nearly identical rejection scenes in Nazareth (textually possible, narratively redundant), or Luke moved the scene for theological reasons.

contradictions.question: Did Herod think Jesus was John the Baptist?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 14:1-2 and Mark 6:14-16 report Herod Antipas concluding that Jesus is John the Baptist resurrected — "It is John, whom I beheaded: he is risen from the dead." Luke 9:9 has Herod actively rejecting that identification: he hears the rumor that Jesus might be John risen but says "John have I beheaded: but who is this, of whom I hear such things?" Matthew and Mark have Herod committed to the identification; Luke has him perplexed and skeptical.
contradictions.commentary: This is a smaller contradiction than most in the gospel-harmonization category, but it's a genuine one and it sits in the same redactional pattern that runs through the Synoptic Problem. Mark's Herod is theologically guilt-ridden — he beheaded John, and now sees a Baptist-shaped specter behind every miracle-worker. Matthew preserves Mark's portrait largely intact. Luke deliberately rewrites it: his Herod is curious rather than haunted, perplexed rather than committed, and the question "but who is this?" sets up the later Lukan motif of Herod's desire to see Jesus (Luke 23:8) and the unique Lukan trial scene before Herod (Luke 23:6-12). The apologist harmonization (Bock, Marshall, Blomberg) reads the difference as character development — Herod initially wavered between several theories about Jesus (one of the old prophets, Elijah, John), eventually settling on the John-the-Baptist theory in Matthew/Mark after more reflection. This is plausible at the psychological level but it ignores the chronological structure of the texts. The Luke 9:9 perplexity and the Matthew 14:2 / Mark 6:16 firm identification are reports of the same moment in the narrative — Herod's reaction upon first hearing of Jesus' miracles. Critical scholarship (Marcus, Fitzmyer, Bovon) reads this as a typical Lukan editorial intervention: Luke softens the Markan portrait of Herod's haunted certainty to set up his later Herod scenes and to leave room for the curious-rather-than-condemned Herod of the Passion narrative. Same source, different theological needs, different result. The contradiction is at the level of "what did Herod conclude" rather than "what did Herod know," but the texts are still contradictory on the conclusion. That is of course a redactional judgment, but Luke is doing what Luke consistently does with Markan material.

contradictions.question: Does the Bible approve of capital punishment?
contradictions.summary: The Pentateuchal legal codes prescribe death by stoning, burning, or general execution for an enormous range of offenses: murder (Gen 9:6; Num 35:30), striking or cursing a parent (Exod 21:15, 17), witchcraft (Exod 22:18), bestiality (Exod 22:19), idolatry (Exod 22:20), Sabbath-breaking (Exod 31:14-15; 35:2), adultery (Lev 20:10), incest (Lev 20:11-14), male homosexuality (Lev 20:13), blasphemy (Lev 24:16), kidnapping (Exod 21:16), loss of virginity before marriage (Deut 22:13-21), and rape victims who didn't cry out loudly enough (Deut 22:23-24). Genesis 4:15 has God explicitly *prevent* the execution of Cain — the first murderer — by placing a protective mark on him. The same canon both prescribes death for dozens of offenses and protects the prototypical murderer from execution.
contradictions.commentary: The question is framed as a binary yes/no, and at that level the answer is unambiguous: the Pentateuch overwhelmingly endorses capital punishment for a long catalog of offenses. Genesis 4:15 is the single anomalous data point, and it sits in a different narrative register — a pre-Sinai etiological story rather than a legal prescription. The apologist harmonization (Walton, Hamilton, Wenham, Sailhamer) reads Genesis 4:15 not as a divine disapproval of capital punishment but as a specific narrative provision protecting Cain from blood-revenge in the pre-Noahic era, before the institution of human juridical authority that Genesis 9:6 establishes ("by man shall his blood be shed"). On this reading, God's protection of Cain is consistent with the later Levitical legal framework because Cain lives in a pre-legal time when no institutional authority exists to execute him; the mark prevents private vengeance, not institutional justice. That's a defensible canonical reading and Walton and Hamilton are reasonable in advancing it. The deeper contradiction, though, is between the Pentateuchal death-penalty catalog and the New Testament Jesus, who in John 8:7 explicitly suspends a Mosaic capital sentence with "he that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her" — a passage that is itself textually problematic (the pericope adulterae is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is a clear later addition to John, but the sentiment is preserved across multiple later witnesses). The actual binary the contradictions database is asking — "does the Bible approve capital punishment" — gets answered yes by the Pentateuch and complicated by the New Testament. Within the Pentateuchal frame alone, the prescriptions vastly outweigh Genesis 4:15, and most critical scholarship (Levenson, Knohl, Milgrom) reads the Holiness Code and the Covenant Code as straightforward endorsements of capital punishment. The contradiction is real if you read the canon as a unified ethical voice; less sharp if you read it as a layered legal tradition with development over time. That is of course a methodological choice. NOTE ON DATA: bibleReferences for answer id=931 contain malformed entries — "Numbers 35.30" (period instead of colon) and "Ex.31:14" (abbreviation). contradictions.question: How did Peter find out that Jesus was the Messiah?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 16:16-17 has Peter confess Jesus as "the Christ, the Son of the living God" at Caesarea Philippi, and Jesus explicitly tells Peter this knowledge came directly by divine revelation: "flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven." John 1:40-41 has Peter learn the identification from a human source: his brother Andrew runs to him and announces, "We have found the Messias." Same conclusion, two incompatible mechanisms — divine revelation in Matthew, ordinary fraternal report in John.
contradictions.commentary: This contradiction reads especially sharply because Matthew goes out of his way to deny exactly the mechanism John gives. The phrase *sarx kai haima ouk apekalypsen soi* ("flesh and blood did not reveal it to you") is unique to Matthew and is a deliberate exclusion of human informants — Jesus is specifically denying that any person told Peter who Jesus was. John, in chapter 1, has Andrew supply precisely that human-informant disclosure. The apologist harmonization (Carson, Köstenberger, Blomberg) typically runs through one of two moves. First, the two-stages move: Andrew gave Peter a preliminary identification of Jesus as the Messiah in John 1, but Peter's full christological confession in Matthew 16 ("the Christ, the Son of the living God") is a deeper revelation that goes beyond what Andrew supplied. Second, the different-events move: John 1 records Peter's initial encounter, Matthew 16 records a separate later moment of fuller insight. These harmonizations have some merit at the surface level. The two-stages move correctly notes that the Matthean confession adds "Son of the living God," which goes beyond Andrew's simple "we have found the Messias." But Matthew 16:17 doesn't say Peter received an *expansion* of an existing identification — it says the revelation came from the Father and not from flesh and blood, which would include Andrew. If Peter had originally learned the basic Messiah-identification from Andrew, Jesus' statement would be false. The most parsimonious reading, and the one critical scholarship (Brown, Meier, Davies-Allison) adopts, is that the Synoptic and Johannine traditions preserve incompatible chronologies of how the disciples came to recognize Jesus' identity. John's gospel front-loads christological recognition into chapter 1; the Synoptics distribute it across the ministry and place the climax at Caesarea Philippi. Brown's commentary on John explicitly notes that the Synoptic delayed-recognition structure and the Johannine immediate-recognition structure cannot be historically reconciled and serve different theological agendas. That is of course a redaction-critical conclusion, but Matthew's denial of human informants is what creates the contradiction with John's report of one.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus forewarn the apostles of his death and resurrection?
contradictions.summary: The Synoptic Gospels record Jesus making at least three explicit, detailed passion predictions to the disciples (Matt 16:21; 17:22-23; 20:18-19; Mark 8:31; 9:31; 10:33-34; Luke 9:22; 9:44; 18:31-33) — each one specifying betrayal, condemnation, death, and resurrection on the third day. John 20:9 then says, after the resurrection, "For as yet they knew not the scripture, that he must rise again from the dead." If Jesus had personally told them three times that he would rise on the third day, John 20:9 is incomprehensible.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleaner cases where the Synoptic and Johannine narrative traditions can't both be reporting the same disciple-knowledge state. The Synoptic passion predictions are increasingly specific — by Mark 10:33-34, Jesus is naming the betrayal, the Gentile transfer, the mocking, the scourging, the death, and the third-day resurrection. The disciples' shock and confusion in the resurrection narratives only makes sense if they hadn't been told. John 20:9 makes this explicit. The apologist harmonization (Carson, Köstenberger, Blomberg, France) runs through the "hidden from them" route: the disciples were told but didn't understand because the meaning was supernaturally hidden from them until after the resurrection. There is genuine textual support for this — Luke 9:45 says "they understood not this saying, and it was hid from them, that they perceived it not." Luke 18:34 repeats: "they understood none of these things: and this saying was hid from them." So the Synoptic tradition itself contains a built-in mechanism for explaining the disciples' incomprehension. The harmonization mitigates the contradiction but doesn't dissolve it. John 20:9 doesn't say the disciples had been told and didn't understand; it says "as yet they knew not the scripture, that he must rise again from the dead" — pointing to scriptural unfamiliarity, not to a forgotten teaching from Jesus. If Jesus had explicitly told them "on the third day I will rise," the post-resurrection problem wouldn't be scriptural ignorance; it would be remembering Jesus' words. Critical scholarship (Brown, Meier, Ehrman, Marcus) widely treats the detailed passion predictions as Markan vaticinia ex eventu — prophecies written after the fact and put into Jesus' mouth to demonstrate his foreknowledge. The disciples' apparent ignorance in the post-resurrection narratives, including John 20:9, is a residue of the historical situation where these predictions did not exist in the form the gospels later supplied them. That is of course a critical-historical judgment, but the Lukan "hidden from them" explanation reads as exactly the kind of editorial overlay that an early redactor adds when his source material contains a contradiction he needs to paper over.

contradictions.question: When did the transfiguration occur?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 17:1 and Mark 9:2 both state that the transfiguration occurred "after six days" following Jesus' prediction about some standing there not tasting death before seeing the kingdom. Luke 9:28 instead reports it occurred "about an eight days after these sayings." Two different numerical intervals between the same saying and the same event.
contradictions.commentary: This is the smallest contradiction in this batch and it's the one with the most defensible apologist harmonization. The apologist response (Marshall, Bock, Carson, Geisler-Howe) reads Luke's "about eight days" (*hōsei hēmerai oktō*) as a Hellenistic inclusive count — Luke is including both the day of the saying and the day of the transfiguration in his count, while Matthew and Mark use an exclusive count of only the days *between* the two events. Six days exclusive + two bracketing days = eight days inclusive. This is genuinely how Greco-Roman authors sometimes counted, and Luke does seem to favor inclusive counting elsewhere (compare his "three days" resurrection count, which uses inclusive reckoning to make Friday-to-Sunday work). The qualifier *hōsei* ("about, approximately") also softens Luke's number to a rough estimate rather than a precise count, which mitigates the contradiction further. Marshall's NIGTC Luke and Bock's BECNT both make this case competently. So this is a place where the harmonization actually has strong textual traction. Critical scholarship (Fitzmyer, Bovon, Marcus) is split — some accept the inclusive/exclusive harmonization as the most parsimonious reading, while others (Fitzmyer) suggest Luke may have simply rounded the figure to the eighth-day theological motif (compare Luke's interest in eight-day periods elsewhere). The contradiction here is genuine at the level of surface arithmetic but probably resolvable at the level of ancient counting conventions. It is one of the weakest contradictions in the SAB list — the kind of "contradiction" that an honest critical reading should flag as defensible by harmonization rather than oversold as a slam-dunk inconsistency. That is of course a subjective judgment about which contradictions are strong, but the inclusive/exclusive convention is real Hellenistic Greek practice and Luke uses it elsewhere.

contradictions.question: Did the disciples understand when Jesus told them about his coming death?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 17:22-23 reports the disciples' reaction to Jesus' second passion prediction: "they were exceeding sorry" (*elypēthēsan sphodra*), indicating comprehension — they understood the message well enough to grieve. The Markan parallel (Mark 9:30-31) and Lukan parallel (Luke 9:44-45) report the opposite: "they understood not that saying, and were afraid to ask him" / "they understood not this saying, and it was hid from them." Matthew has the disciples grieving in comprehension; Mark and Luke have them confused and afraid to ask.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction here is internal to the Synoptic tradition and it's a clear case of Matthean editorial smoothing. Mark, the source for both Matthew and Luke at this point, reports incomprehension and fear. Luke follows Mark and intensifies the incomprehension ("hidden from them, that they perceived it not"). Matthew removes the incomprehension entirely and substitutes a comprehension-with-grief reaction. The apologist harmonization (Carson, Blomberg, Hagner) splits the difference: the disciples partially understood (enough to be grieved) but didn't fully grasp the meaning (enough to remain confused). On this reading, all three gospels are reporting a partial-comprehension state, with each evangelist emphasizing a different aspect. That harmonization has some psychological plausibility — partial understanding plus emotional reaction plus persistent confusion is a coherent state of mind. But it strains the Greek. Mark 9:32 says *ēgnooun to rhēma* — "they were not knowing the saying" — using *agnoeō*, which means actual non-comprehension, not partial understanding. Luke 9:45 doubles down with *parakekalymmenon* ("covered over, veiled") and *hina mē aisthōntai auto* ("so that they might not perceive it"). Matthew's *elypēthēsan sphodra* ("they were greatly grieved") presupposes the opposite — they got the message clearly enough to be devastated by it. Critical scholarship (Marcus, Davies-Allison, Bovon) reads this as a typical Matthean upgrade of the disciples' competence — Matthew systematically reduces the disciples' confusion compared to his Markan source, presenting them as a more theologically responsive inner circle. Davies-Allison documents this pattern throughout Matthew's gospel. The contradiction is at the level of "did they understand or not," and Matthew and Mark/Luke give incompatible answers about the same conversation. The partial-comprehension harmonization papers over the surface-level conflict but doesn't account for the directional editorial change critical scholarship has documented. That is of course a redaction-critical judgment, but Matthew's habit of upgrading disciple-competence is well-attested.
